newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Talks end without clearer picture of Zaire force.
newsitem.headline: Talks end without clearer picture of Zaire force.

text.p: Rebels in eastern Zaire allowed U.N. officials access to assess aid needs for war refugees but plans for a multinational protection force for the area looked no clearer after strategy talks in Germany.
Western and African military officials who met in Stuttgart agreed on scenarios to help refugees in Zaire but there was no obvious note of urgency in their decisions.

Support for the French-backed plan has been waning since about half a million Hutu refugees returned home to Rwanda en masse just over a week ago. They streamed out after ethnic Tutsi rebels chased out armed Hutu hardliners preventing them from leaving refugee camps in Zaire sheltering them since 1994.

Some Western nations, notably the United States, felt the need for a military force inside Zaire had diminished since Hutus were able to return to the homeland they fled in 1994. Hutus fear revenge for the massacre of Rwanda Tutsis that year.
The Stuttgart meeting appeared largely to be a gesture to those like France pressing for intervention to help hundreds of thousands of refugees still believed to be roaming the bush.
But in the end the military leaders avoided specific decisions, agreeing scenarios ranging from sending no new troops to using a multinational force to protect refugees if necessary.

They did not specify how many troops might be needed under any of the options, which must now go to political leaders for consideration. They also did not say where a mission could be based or what soldiers' rules of engagement might be.

"The mission of a multinational force, as we have defined it, would be to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian assistance and voluntary repatriation of refugees and displaced persons," said General Maurice Baril of Canada, who has been named to head any multinational force.
"The objectives of such a force would be strictly humanitarian. The force would be politically and militarily neutral."
Baril told reporters the three-day talks came to a consensus that at least 250,000 refugees were still in eastern Zaire.
This was close to a U.S. estimate released on Saturday of 202,000 but far below estimates of around 700,000 from aid groups and the United Nations High Commission for Refugees.
The meeting, held at U.S. European Command in Germany, concluded that up to 300,000 more refugees may still be in eastern Zaire but that there was no confirmation of this.
In eastern Zaire itself, officials of the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said they had begun assessing the need for aid to refugees after finally being allowed access by rebels.
"We started today our assessment," UNHCR spokesman Mans Nyberg told Reuters on Sunday. "Today they are mainly operating in Bukavu but tomorrow they will go elsewhere in the area."

The rebels agreed on Saturday to allow into Zaire the UNHCR and other relief organisations, who believe hundreds of thousands of Rwandan refugees are still in Zaire and badly in need of humanitarian aid.
The rebels say there are very few refugees left after the Hutu exodus.

The Tutsi rebels launched an armed campaign on October 18, ostensibly to fight for their citizenship rights. They now say they want to topple the government of Zaire's ailing President Mobutu Sese Seseko, who marked 31 years in power on Sunday.
The rebels fear an intervention force could end up shoring up Mobutu, and have vowed to fight foreign troops.
